reference.source: Textbook of Pediatric Rheumatology / ILAR & PRINTO criteria
clinicalPearls: Defined under the ILAR framework as arthritis affecting four or fewer joints in the first six months, subclassified into persistent (never more than four joints) and extended (spreading to five or more thereafter) forms
Typically affects young girls, often with a positive antinuclear antibody, and commonly involves large joints such as the knee and ankle asymmetrically
The chief long-term threat is chronic anterior uveitis, which is frequently insidious and asymptomatic (white eye) yet sight-threatening
Regular slit-lamp surveillance is essential, with the highest uveitis risk in young, antinuclear-antibody-positive girls with early disease onset
A swollen, warm but often surprisingly non-tender knee with a limp and morning stiffness is a common presentation
Limb-length discrepancy and localised overgrowth can occur because chronic inflammation accelerates growth at the affected joint
First-line treatment is NSAIDs and intra-articular corticosteroids, with methotrexate reserved for persistent or extended disease and uveitis
reference.pathophysiology: Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is a chronic, immune-mediated synovitis in which T-cell-driven inflammation of the synovial membrane produces effusion, pannus formation and, if untreated, cartilage and bone damage. The strong association with antinuclear antibody positivity and chronic anterior uveitis suggests shared autoreactivity between synovial and uveal tissue. Chronic hyperaemia around an inflamed joint can stimulate the adjacent growth plate, producing localised overgrowth and limb-length inequality, while unchecked synovitis eventually causes erosive joint damage in the extended subtype.
additionalDifferentials: Malignancy (leukaemia, neuroblastoma) causing joint or bone pain
Other JIA subtypes including enthesitis-related arthritis
additionalInvestigations: Antinuclear antibody to stratify uveitis risk
Inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein), which may be normal or only mildly raised
Joint ultrasound or MRI to confirm synovitis and assess disease extent
Slit-lamp ophthalmological examination at diagnosis and on a scheduled surveillance basis
Joint aspiration and synovial fluid analysis when infection is a concern
Full blood count and film to help exclude malignancy
Rheumatoid factor and HLA-B27 to help distinguish other subtypes
redFlags: Painless progressive visual loss or band keratopathy indicating chronic uveitis complications
Fever, severe pain or systemic upset suggesting infection or malignancy
Nocturnal bone pain and cytopenias raising concern for leukaemia
Rapid spread to many joints suggesting extended or polyarticular evolution
reference.prognosis: The persistent form often has a favourable articular outcome, whereas the extended form carries a higher risk of erosive joint damage and disability. Uveitis, if undetected, can cause cataract, glaucoma and permanent visual loss, making ophthalmic surveillance the key determinant of long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Relying on the child to report eye symptoms, when sight-threatening uveitis is frequently asymptomatic
Assuming normal inflammatory markers exclude active arthritis
Missing limb-length discrepancy and consequent gait or postural problems
Failing to reassess for extension of joint involvement over time
Overlooking infection or malignancy in an atypical monoarthritis
references: ILAR classification of juvenile idiopathic arthritis
management: Intra-articular corticosteroid injection is the mainstay for active oligoarthritis, combined with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for symptom relief
Escalate to methotrexate for persistent or extended disease, and to biologic agents such as tumour necrosis factor inhibitors for refractory arthritis or uveitis

Scheduled slit-lamp surveillance for chronic anterior uveitis stratified by antinuclear-antibody status and age, treated with topical corticosteroids and, if needed, methotrexate or a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy to preserve joint function, muscle strength and range of movement
Monitor and manage limb-length discrepancy and localised overgrowth with orthotics and orthopaedic input
Multidisciplinary paediatric rheumatology and ophthalmology care with disease-modifying drug safety monitoring
